summary: Adapts the X.500 subentry mechanism for use with LDAP. In X.500 directories, subentries are special entries that hold information associated with a subtree or subtree refinement. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A directory is like a tree of folders. A subentry is a special note stuck to a branch holding rules or facts that apply to everything under that branch.

questions: what is a subentry in a directory
what is the ldap subentries control
subtitle: How LDAP carries X.500 subentries, the special entries that describe administrative rules for part of the directory tree.

tldr.problem: X.500 directories use subentries to hold administrative information about a subtree, and LDAP needed a standard way to represent and search them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the Subtree Specification syntax, the administrativeRole and subtreeSpecification attributes, the subentry object class, and a subentries control that changes whether searches see subentries or normal entries.
tldr.outcome: Subentries follow X.501 behavior in LDAP and are hidden from one-level and subtree searches unless the control is used. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3672 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2003, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What a Subentry Is
sections.content:
The RFC quotes X.501: a subentry is a special kind of entry immediately subordinate to an administrative point. It holds attributes that pertain to a subtree, or subtree refinement, associated with that administrative point. A single subentry may serve all or several aspects of administrative authority, or each aspect may have its own subentries.

In LDAP, subentries SHALL behave as X.501 describes unless this RFC says otherwise. The main difference is visibility. Without the subentries control, subentries SHALL NOT be considered in one-level and subtree scope searches, but they are considered for all other operations, including base scope searches.
sections.plainLanguage: A subentry is a hidden note attached to a branch of the tree. Normal searches skip the notes, but if you point right at one, you can read it.

sections.title: Subtree Specification Syntax
sections.content:
The Subtree Specification syntax names a set of entries inside a subtree of the Directory Information Tree. If the set is not one contiguous subtree, it is called a subtree refinement. The LDAP syntax OID is 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.45, and values are encoded with the Generic String Encoding Rules (RFC 3641). Appendix A gives an equivalent ABNF.

The ASN.1 type has these parts:

  • base: the starting entry, relative to the root of the scope; absent means the scope root itself.
  • specificExclusions: entries to cut out, either chopBefore (the entry and its subordinates) or chopAfter (only its subordinates).
  • minimum and maximum: depth limits in RDN arcs below the base; minimum defaults to 0 and an absent maximum means no limit.
  • specificationFilter: a boolean expression over objectClass values using item, and, or and not.

An empty sequence {} includes every entry within scope.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a way to say which branches count: start here, skip these twigs, go no deeper than this, and only include certain kinds of leaves.

sections.title: Attributes and Object Class
sections.content:
The administrativeRole operational attribute (OID 2.5.18.5) marks an entry as an administrative point and says which roles its area serves. It also limits which kinds of subentry may sit below it. The X.501 values are autonomousArea, accessControlSpecificArea, accessControlInnerArea, subschemaAdminSpecificArea, collectiveAttributeSpecificArea and collectiveAttributeInnerArea.

The subtreeSpecification operational attribute (OID 2.5.18.6) is single-valued and present in all subentries. The subentry object class (OID 2.5.17.0) is structural, has top as superior, and requires cn and subtreeSpecification.
sections.plainLanguage: One label says this branch has rules. Each rule note must have a name and a description of which branches it covers.

sections.title: The Subentries Control
sections.content:
A client MAY attach the subentries control to a search request to choose what is visible. Its controlType is 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.10.1, its criticality may be TRUE or FALSE, and its controlValue is a BER-encoded BOOLEAN that MUST be present. TRUE means subentries are visible and normal entries are not. FALSE means normal entries are visible and subentries are not.

TRUE encodes as the three octets 01 01 FF and FALSE as 01 01 00. There is no response control, and the control is not appropriate for operations other than search.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a switch on your search. One position shows only the hidden notes, the other shows only the normal entries.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Subentries often hold administrative or other sensitive information, so they should be protected from unauthorized access and disclosure as described in RFC 2829 and RFC 2830. General LDAP security considerations from RFC 3377 also apply.

IANA has registered the descriptors for the attributes, the object class and the administrative roles, and registered the subentries control as an LDAP protocol mechanism. The control OID was assigned by the OpenLDAP Foundation from its private enterprise allocation.
sections.plainLanguage: The hidden notes can hold private rules, so only the right people should be allowed to read them.
